body:
I don't understand what this is proposing. If we expose `CustomStateSet` on elements, wouldn't that mean that a user of a custom element can override its internal state?

Also, why does it mean that authors cannot remove a state through `ElementInternals` anymore? I don't understand why that is the case, but if that were to be the case, that seems like a breaking change that we cannot make.

@annevk Perhaps I didn't explain it well. These are different sets. The resulting states that would be matched by `:state()` would be a **union** of states specified across `ElementInternals`, `element.states` or even a potential [CSS custom states API](https://github.com/w3c/csswg-drafts/issues/12502). WC authors can absolutely remove states they've set on `ElementInternals`, but if the same state applies through some other mechanism, `:state(foo)` would still match.

I see this as no different than being able to apply a default `role` via `ElementInternals` and component consumers being able to override it by setting the `role` attribute directly on component instances.

Why is this better than using `classList` and dot-prefixed selectors? You state "There are many use cases where one needs to target elements using a CSS selector, without touching their DOM." Could you give an example of such a case?

Seems to me that there are two good reasons to want to avoid classlist:

1. You want to avoid "sprouting attributes", which can cause for e.g. mutation observers to update. 
2. You want to have full control of when the state is toggled on/off. 

If you don't care about either `classList` is fine. If you only care about 1, custom states might be a very big hammer to hit the nail, considering you could probably do similar things with CSS' custom properties and style queries IIRC.

I think Domenic's question around 1 is valid though: what are the compelling use-cases that justify such a change.

The problems I see with 2 are:

- `attachInternals()` is a grab bag of lots of internal things which we don't want to expose on any element (e.g. `.shadowRoot`). 
- Having some other method like `.attachStateSet()` might be fine, but...
- Interleaving multiple statesets such as those from `attachInternals()` is probably a non-starter; it violates the principle of full control for custom element authors if states can be clobbered by some new thing.
- In practice I wonder how often people would reach for something like `.attachStateSet()` if it throws an error on the second call. This is different for custom elements where the lifecycle hooks are tightly controlled. How can you guarantee your code is the first code to call `.attachStateSet()` in a large application?

> I see this as no different than being able to apply a default `role` via `ElementInternals` and component consumers being able to override it by setting the `role` attribute directly on component instances.

I think role conceptually different, as well as different in practice. For one, the `role=` attribute takes precedent over `.attachInternals().role` as you mention, but this isn't a desirable property for CSS custom states. Secondly `.attachInternals().role = ` would throw on non-custom elements also. Lastly I haven't seen folks asking for the equivalent of `.attachInternals().role=` for non-custom elements; I imagine this is because they would just use the `role=` attribute, which I guess brings us in a circle wrt custom-states and classes.

@domenic 
> Why is this better than using `classList` and dot-prefixed selectors? You state "There are many use cases where one needs to target elements using a CSS selector, without touching their DOM." Could you give an example of such a case?

The high-level use case is styling elements you don't control, where touching their DOM in an observable way is seen as obtrusive, and in some cases actively incompatible with tooling that doesn't expect it (e.g. React is notorious for not preserving DOM changes by third parties).

More concrete examples:
- Attaching state to slotted elements and their descendants without requiring authors to switch to another custom element created entirely for this purpose. E.g. `img:state(loading)` for slotted avatars in an `<avatar-group>` component.
- Browser extensions, third-party UI libraries styling DOM elements a certain way without interfering with the page's mutation observers and other selectors.
- Custom attributes, once we have them
- Libraries, CSS frameworks etc that need to be able to style a class of elements without modifying DOM

@keithamus 
> it violates the principle of full control for custom element authors if states can be clobbered by some new thing.

Where is this principle and what is its scope? Many other things set by `ElementInternals` can be "clobbered" by regular DOM methods (e.g. `role`), and it doesn't come up as a problem. Do you have a concrete example where this would be an issue?

> I think role conceptually different, as well as different in practice. For one, the `role=` attribute takes precedent over `.attachInternals().role` as you mention, but this isn't a desirable property for CSS custom states. 

Why is it not a desirable property for CSS custom states?

> Lastly I haven't seen folks asking for the equivalent of `.attachInternals().role=` for non-custom elements; I imagine this is because they would just use the `role=` attribute, which I guess brings us in a circle wrt custom-states and classes.

Yes, because `role` is not inherently an `ElementInternals` concept, `ElementInternals` just lets you set defaults. I see states as exactly the same, whereas you seem to see them as inherently an `ElementInternals` concept that does not make sense outside it (which is evident in your proposed API too, which is framed around attachment — a very WC-centric view). Why?
